lead: At 11 km the air outside is thin and cold. A crew cannot breathe it, and the lungs cannot pull enough oxygen out of it. So the cabin is sealed and fed with conditioned bleed air, while a valve at the rear lets the surplus out at a controlled rate. That valve, not the supply, sets the cabin pressure. The supply itself is hot, so a pack cools it and then expands it through a turbine. Every airliner uses this, from a Chennai–Delhi A320 to a long-haul 787.
prereq: You need: the bleed air source and its regulation from Chapter 2.2.

sections.h3: Why the cabin must hold a pressure altitude

blocks.text: At 35 000 ft (10 700 m) the air outside sits at about 23.8 kPa. Sea-level air is 101.3 kPa. Oxygen is 21% of dry air by volume at both heights, so the partial pressure of oxygen falls with the total pressure, from about 21.3 kPa to 5.0 kPa. Blood leaving the lungs cannot pick up enough oxygen at that level. The result is hypoxia: dulled judgement first, then loss of consciousness.

Trapped gas is the second problem. By Boyle's law, p × V is constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature. One litre of gas in the middle ear, a sinus or the gut at 101.3 kPa becomes 101.3 ÷ 23.8 = 4.3 litres at 35 000 ft. The body cannot stretch that far. Ear and sinus pain follow, and tissue can be damaged.

So the cabin is held at a cabin altitude: the altitude in the standard atmosphere whose pressure equals the cabin pressure. The usual limit is 8000 ft (2438 m), where the pressure is 75.6 kPa. The fuselage sets a maximum differential pressure, typically about 55–60 kPa (8–9 psi) on an airliner.
Δp = p<sub>cabin</sub> − p<sub>ambient</sub>        F = Δp × A
blocks.where: Δp is the differential pressure in Pa; p<sub>cabin</sub> is the pressure inside the cabin; p<sub>ambient</sub> is the pressure outside at the aircraft's altitude; F is the outward force on a panel in N; A is the panel area in m².

blocks.text: Design lives between the two limits. At cruise the cabin sits near 8000 ft and Δp is large, so the structure carries a heavy steady load. If the aircraft climbs higher, or the cabin cannot hold its pressure, the cabin altitude rises and the crew must act. Oxygen for that case is Chapter 2.8.

sections.h3: The outflow valve sets the pressure

blocks.text: The fuselage is a pressure vessel with doors and many seals. It is not airtight, and it should not be. Air enters from the packs at a controlled mass flow and leaves through one large opening near the rear, the outflow valve. That valve is a motor-driven gate or butterfly. Open it and cabin pressure falls. Close it and pressure rises. The supply only has to exceed the natural leak plus the outflow.

The cabin pressure controller reads cabin pressure from its own sensors, takes static pressure from the air data system, and drives the valve to follow a schedule. The crew selects a target cabin altitude and a rate of change, or lets the automatic schedule fly it.

items: Ground: valve fully open, cabin at field elevation, no differential, so the door can be opened safely.
Takeoff: the valve closes progressively after liftoff, so the cabin does not bump.
Climb: cabin altitude climbs at a limited rate, a few hundred feet per minute, to keep ears comfortable, until 8000 ft.
Cruise: cabin altitude held constant while the aircraft climbs or steps.
Descent: cabin altitude comes down so that at touchdown it equals field elevation, and the valve opens as outside pressure rises.
Manual: the crew drives the valve directly if the automatic channel fails.

blocks.text: Three protections sit outside the controller. The positive pressure relief valve opens outward if Δp passes the structural limit. The negative pressure relief valve opens inward if outside pressure is higher than inside, for example after a rapid descent or a landing with the cabin still pressurised. A dump switch opens the valve fully on the ground, used for smoke removal.

sections.h3: Air cycle cooling: expand the air and it cools

blocks.text: Bleed air leaves the engine at roughly 200 °C and 2–3 bar. It must reach the cabin at a comfortable temperature, so a pack cools it. The pack uses no refrigerant; it uses the air itself. Three effects share the work: heat transfer to ram air, compression, and expansion.

items: Flow control valve: meters bleed air and holds the pack to its design mass flow.
Primary heat exchanger: ram air from a scoop removes heat.
Compressor: the air is squeezed again. It leaves hotter, but at higher pressure.
Secondary heat exchanger: ram air removes that heat, so the air leaves cooler than it did after the primary.
Turbine: the air expands through a wheel and does work on it. The work drives the compressor on the same shaft. Air that has given up energy leaves the turbine very cold, near 0 °C or below.
Water separator: condensed water is spun or coalesced out, so no fog or ice reaches the cabin.

blocks.text: Why does expansion cool? Cooling means energy leaves the air. In the turbine the air pushes the blades and hands over energy as shaft work, so its temperature drops steeply. Simply forcing the same air through a hole gives almost no cooling, because the energy stays in the gas. That is why a pack has a turbine and not a nozzle.

In the bootstrap cycle the turbine drives the compressor through a shaft, which is the arrangement above. In the simple cycle there is no compressor: heat exchanger, then turbine. It gives less cooling and is used where bleed pressure is low and demand is small.

The pack delivers air colder than needed. A temperature control valve lets hot bleed air bypass the pack, and zone trim valves mix it into each cabin zone. Ram air flow comes from a fan on the turbine shaft on the ground, or from a modulating flap in flight.

figure.caption: Bleed air runs down the pack: metered, cooled, compressed, cooled again, then expanded in the turbine, the stage that makes it cold. Water is removed before the cabin, whose pressure is set by the outflow valve at the end.

spec.title: Air cycle pack
spec.aria: Bleed air is metered, cooled in two heat exchangers with compression in between, then cooled sharply by expansion in the turbine before water is removed and the air enters the cabin.

examples.question: An aircraft cruises at 35 000 ft, where the ambient pressure is 23.8 kPa. The cabin is held at 8000 ft, where the pressure is 75.6 kPa. (a) Find the differential pressure in kPa and in psi. (b) Find the outward force on a plug-type door of area 1.2 m². Take 1 psi = 6.895 kPa.
steps: List the data: p_cabin = 75.6 kPa, p_ambient = 23.8 kPa, A = 1.2 m².
Convert to base units: 51.8 kPa = 51 800 Pa.
Comment: the door is held by stops, and this steady load passes into the fuselage frames and skins.
examples.answer: Differential pressure 51.8 kPa (7.5 psi); outward force on the door 62.2 kN.
examples.check:
p_cab = 75.6
p_amb = 23.8
A = 1.2
dp = p_cab - p_amb
print(round(dp, 1))
print(round(dp / 6.895, 1))
print(round(dp * 1000 * A / 1000, 1))

traps: Saying the pack compressor cools the air. It heats it. The turbine cools it, because the air gives up shaft work there.
Saying the supply pressure sets the cabin pressure. The outflow valve sets it; the supply only has to cover the leak plus the outflow.
Mixing cabin altitude with aircraft altitude. The cabin is at 8000 ft while the aircraft is at 35 000 ft, and the difference drives the door load.
Unit slips in Δp × A: kPa must become Pa (×1000) before multiplying by area in m², or the force comes out 1000 times too small.
Reversing the relief valves. The positive relief valve opens outward on excess Δp; the negative relief valve opens inward when outside pressure wins.

quiz.q: State the usual maximum cabin altitude and the pressure that goes with it.
quiz.a: 8000 ft (2438 m), where the standard atmosphere pressure is 75.6 kPa.

quiz.q: Why does the cabin need pressurising at all, when the percentage of oxygen in air does not change with height?
quiz.a: Oxygen is still 21% by volume, but the total pressure falls, so the partial pressure of oxygen falls with it and the lungs cannot load the blood. Gas trapped in ears, sinuses and gut also expands as pressure drops, causing pain.

quiz.q: An aircraft is at 30 000 ft (p = 30.1 kPa) with the cabin at 6000 ft (p = 81.2 kPa). Find Δp and the outward force on a window of area 0.8 m².
The outflow valve jams closed during descent. What happens to Δp, which valve protects the structure, and what should the crew do?
quiz.a: Outside pressure rises while the cabin stays at its old pressure, so Δp falls and then reverses, leaving the cabin below ambient. The negative pressure relief valve opens inward to stop a reverse differential building. The crew selects manual control or uses the dump function to open the valve, and descends gently to limit the cabin rate.

quiz.q: Name the two heat exchangers in a bootstrap pack and state what removes the heat in each.
quiz.a: The primary heat exchanger and the secondary heat exchanger; both reject heat to ram air from a scoop.

quiz.q: Why is the water separator placed after the turbine and not before it?
quiz.a: Water condenses only when the air becomes cold, and the air is coldest at the turbine exit. Separating it there stops fog in the cabin and ice in the ducts and valves downstream.

quiz.q: A type has a maximum differential pressure of 55 kPa and holds the cabin at 75.6 kPa. At what ambient pressure is the limit reached, and what must the controller do above that altitude?
quiz.a: p_ambient = 75.6 − 55 = 20.6 kPa. Above the altitude where ambient pressure is 20.6 kPa, the controller must let the cabin altitude rise with the aircraft so that Δp stays at the limit; the cabin can no longer be held at 8000 ft.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer aircraft push two limits: the 787 takes bleed air out of the pressurisation loop and drives the packs with electric compressors, and some types hold a lower cabin altitude, near 6000 ft, to reduce fatigue on long flights. Cabin air quality is an active research area, covering ozone converters, volatile organic compounds from engine oil and hydraulic fluid, and filtration. Search for "bleedless environmental control system", "cabin altitude 6000 ft" and "cabin air quality" if you want to read further.
